pattern.description: Search pattern (regex or literal string)

path.description: Directory or file to search (default: current directory)

glob.description: Filter files by glob pattern, e.g. '*.ts' or '**/*.spec.ts'

literal.description: Treat pattern as literal string instead of regex (default: false)

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (default: 0)

limit.description: Maximum number of matches to return (default: 100)

toolsAdded.name: find
toolsAdded.description: Search for files by glob pattern. Returns matching file paths relative to the search directory. Respects .gitignore. Output is truncated to 1000 results or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match files, e.g. '*.ts', '**/*.json', or 'src/**/*.spec.ts'

path.description: Directory to search in (default: current directory)

limit.description: Maximum number of results (default: 1000)

toolsAdded.description: List directory contents. Returns entries sorted alphabetically, with '/' suffix for directories. Includes dotfiles. Output is truncated to 500 entries or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

path.description: Directory to list (default: current directory)

limit.description: Maximum number of entries to return (default: 500)

sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.

- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)

Every edit is saved to the server (debounced) into a JSON file on disk, so the text is still there after a page reload, a browser restart, an incognito window, or a server restart. ## Fixed design decisions (do not re-litigate during implementation) 1. **Server-side persistence to a file, not `localStorage`.** `localStorage` would satisfy 'persist across sessions' only per-browser and is invisible to automated verification. A file store gives an observable artifact (`data/hello.json`), survives server restarts and works across browsers/devices. See Risks R1 for the rejected alternative. 2. **Zero runtime and zero dev dependencies.** Node 26.8.1 is installed (mise) and provides `node:http`, `node:fs` and the built-in test runner `node --test`. Playwright 1.63.0 + Chromium 1228 are already installed globally (`~/.local/share/mise/installs/npm-playwright/1.63.0`, browsers in `~/.cache/ms-playwright`); `VALIDATION.md` explicitly forbids installing browser packages that already exist. Do not add React/Vite/Express/Tailwind/Prettier/ESLint. 3. **Editing via `contenteditable="plaintext-only"` on an `

`.** Read and write **only `textContent`**, never `innerHTML` — this is both the XSS boundary and what keeps stored data plain text. Browsers without `plaintext-only` fall back to `true`; since we always save/read `textContent`, pasted markup is flattened on save anyway. 4. **Single user, last-write-wins.** No auth, no sessions, no CRDT, no optimistic-concurrency ETags. Documented as an explicit assumption (R3). 5. **Default text is exactly `hello world`** (lowercase, one space). ## File layout to create ``` package.json # type=module, scripts: start | test | check ; no dependencies main.js # entry point: wires store + server, reads PORT/DATA_FILE env, listens store.js # file-backed text store: createFileStore(path) -> {read, write} server.js # createServer(store) -> http.Server ; routing + JSON API ; no listen() public/index.html # markup: h1#text contenteditable, status pill, layer elements public/app.js # load text, edit, debounced save, status indicator public/styles.css # the visual design (see Visual spec) tests/store.test.js # unit tests for the file store tests/api.test.js # HTTP integration tests via createServer + fetch on port 0 .gitignore # node_modules/, data/ README.md # how to run, how to test, data location, limitations docs/architecture.md # fill in the template: modules, contracts, dependency rule, compromise data/hello.json # runtime-created, gitignored ``` Do **not** touch `init.txt` (pre-existing, empty) or the other `docs/` files. --- ## Steps ### 1. Scaffold → outcome: `npm test` and `npm run check` run cleanly on an empty suite **Files:** `package.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md` - `package.json`: `{ "name": "hello-world", "private": true, "type": "module", "scripts": { "start": "node main.js", "test": "node --test tests/", "check": "node --check store.js && node --check server.js && node --check main.js && node --check public/app.js" } }`. Any other `fs` error propagates (do **not** swallow it — AGENTS §8, coding-standards). - `write(text)` — `mkdirSync(dirname(filePath), { recursive: true })`, write to `filePath + '.tmp'`, then `renameSync` onto `filePath`. The temp+rename is deliberate: it prevents a truncated/corrupt `hello.json` if the process dies mid-write. Only a string is accepted; throw `TypeError` otherwise. - The store owns the path; nothing else in the codebase touches the filesystem. **Tests (`tests/store.test.js`, `node:test` + `node:assert`, each test uses `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(),'hello-'))` and cleans up):** 1. `read()` on a fresh empty dir returns `'hello world'`. 2. `write('bonjour')` then a **new** `createFileStore(samePath)` reads `'bonjour'` (proves on-disk persistence, not memory). 3. HTTP server + JSON API → outcome: `curl` can read and overwrite the greeting **Files:** `server.js`, `main.js`, `tests/api.test.js`, plus a one-line placeholder `public/index.html` (replaced in step 4) **Public contract (implement exactly):** | Method | Path | Response | |---|---|---| | GET | `/` | 200 `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/styles.css` | 200 — `text/css; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/app.js` | 200 — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/api/text` | 200 `{"text":""}` | | PUT | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → 200 `{"text":""}` | | any | other | 404 `{"error":"not found"}` | Error semantics: PUT with unparseable JSON or a non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`. Body larger than `MAX_TEXT_BYTES = 10000` → `413 {"error":"text too long"}` (stop accumulating and consume the rest). Method other than GET/PUT on any path → `405` with an `Allow` header. An unexpected throw from the store → `500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** `console.error` including method, path and the error (never silent). Structure: `server.js` exports `createServer(store)` returning an `http.Server` and never calls `listen` (keeps it testable). Static files are read once from an explicit asset map (`'/'`, `'/styles.css'`, `'/app.js'` → file + content-type) rather than a generic path-resolving static handler — smaller code and no path-traversal surface; note this trade-off in `docs/architecture.md`. `main.js` reads `PORT` (default 3000) and `DATA_FILE` (default `./data/hello.json` resolved from `import.meta.url`), builds the store, listens and logs one startup line: `Editing at http://localhost:3000 (data: /abs/path/data/hello.json)`. **Tests (`tests/api.test.js`)** — build `createServer(createFileStore(join(tmpdir…,'hello.json')))` and `listen(0)` in `before`, close in `after`, use global `fetch`: 1. `GET /` is 200 and `content-type` starts with `text/html`. 2. `GET /api/text` on a fresh store → `{"text":"hello world"}`. 3. `PUT /api/text {"text":"hi there"}` → 200, and a following `GET` returns `"hi there"`. 4. **Restart proof:** close the server, create a *second* server over the same file, `GET` still returns `"hi there"`. 5. `PUT` body `{"text":123}` → 400 with an `error` field. 6. `PUT` body `not json` → 400. 7. `PUT` text of 10001 chars → 413. 8. `DELETE /api/text` → 405 with `allow` header. 9. `GET /nope` → 404. **Test command:** `node --test tests/api.test.js`, then `node --test tests/`. Manual smoke: `PORT=3100 node main.js` + `curl -s localhost:3100/api/text` and `curl -s -X PUT -d '{"text":"x"}' localhost:3100/api/text`; then `cat data/hello.json`. --- ### 4. Editable client → outcome: typing in the headline persists after a reload **Files:** `public/index.html`, `public/app.js` (delete the step-3 placeholder markup) Markup requirements: ``, ``, ``, ``, `hello world`, one `
`, an `

hello world

`, a `

` save indicator, and `

`/`
` nodes in a contenteditable. 7. The client never writes `innerHTML` and never renders stored data as HTML. **Test:** this behaviour is proven by the browser E2E in step 6 (a headless Playwright script), because it is DOM-level; there is no DOM in the Node test runner and we are not adding jsdom. In this step verify manually with `node main.js` in a real browser plus `curl` + `cat data/hello.json`, and confirm the browser console is clean. --- ### 5. Visual design → outcome: a screenshot that would pass as a polished landing hero **Files:** `public/styles.css` (new), `public/index.html` (add the decorative layer elements) Concrete, checkable spec (each item becomes an acceptance criterion or a screenshot check): - **Canvas:** `html,body{height:100%}`, `body{min-height:100svh; display:grid; place-items:center; overflow:hidden; margin:0}`, `color-scheme: dark`, palette in CSS custom properties. Text container `width:min(1100px, 92vw)`, `text-align:center`, `padding: clamp(1rem, 6vw, 4rem)`. - **Layered background** (three stacked layers, all `position:fixed; inset:0; pointer-events:none; z-index:-1`): 1. base `radial-gradient` at 50% 20% `#1b1f4b` → `#0a0a14` over a `linear-gradient` to `#05060d`; 2. three blurred aurora blobs (`.blob` divs, `border-radius:50%`, `filter: blur(90px)`, `opacity:.5`, `mix-blend-mode:screen`, hues violet `#6d5efc`, cyan `#22d3ee`, magenta `#f472b6`), each with a slow `@keyframes drift` (24 s / 33 s / 41 s, `alternate`, translate+scale) and `will-change:transform`; 3. film grain: an inline SVG `feTurbulence` **data-URI** as `background-image` on a pseudo-element at `opacity:.05`, plus a vignette `radial-gradient(transparent 45%, rgba(0,0,0,.55))`. No external images, fonts or CDNs. - **Typography:** `font-family: ui-rounded, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Inter, sans-serif`; `#text{font-size: clamp(3rem, 12vw, 11rem); font-weight:800; letter-spacing:-.04em; line-height:.95}`; `white-space: pre-wrap; overflow-wrap: break-word` so a long edit never overflows. - **Text treatment:** `background: linear-gradient(100deg,#ffffff,#b7c3ff 35%,#7dd3fc 70%,#f0abfc)` + `background-size:220%` + `background-clip:text` + `-webkit-text-fill-color:transparent`, with a 12 s `background-position` animation; add `filter: drop-shadow(0 0 40px rgba(125,211,252,.35))` for glow and **`caret-color:#fff`** so the caret stays visible against the transparent fill. On `#text:focus` add a subtle underline/ring so the editable affordance is discoverable. - **Focus visible:** `#text:focus-visible{ outline:2px solid #7dd3fc; outline-offset:.2em; border-radius:.1em }` (WCAG 2.4.7 — this is a required check, not a nice-to-have). - **Status pill:** fixed `bottom: clamp(1rem,5vh,3rem)`, centred, small uppercase `letter-spacing` label with a coloured dot per state (`.saving`, `.saved`, `.error`), `transition: opacity .3s`, low-opacity by default and higher on change. - **Micro-interaction:** `@keyframes pulse` on `.saved` applied to the pill (and a brief brightness bump on the headline). CSS-only. - **Responsive:** verify at 1440×900 and 390×844 — below 640 px reduce blur to 50 px and confirm **zero horizontal scroll**. - **Reduced motion:** `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){ *,*::before,*::after{ animation:none !important; transition:none !important } }`. - Contrast: all foreground text (status pill, headline) must meet 4.5:1 against its backdrop. - **Out of scope (state explicitly):** a light theme, user-selectable colours/fonts, animations triggered on hover. **Test:** no unit test. Evidence = screenshots captured in step 6 at 1440×900 and 390×844, plus the reduced-motion screenshot; a human reviews them against the checklist above (this is the one criterion that needs human eyes — flag it as such). --- ### 6. End-to-end validation → outcome: the full journey is proven by an automated browser run with zero console errors **Files:** `/tmp/hello-e2e.mjs` (**throwaway — do not commit**, per `VALIDATION.md`: no committed Playwright config/deps/tests). Playwright is already installed globally. Import it from the absolute path `~/.local/share/mise/installs/npm-playwright/1.63.0/node_modules/playwright/index.js` (Chromium 1228 is already in `~/.cache/ms-playwright`). If that import path fails, `playwright screenshot` from the mise shim is the fallback for screenshots only, and the persistence journey must then be proven with `curl` + `cat data/hello.json` with the blocker disclosed. Start the app (`PORT=3100 node main.js`, backgrounded, capture stdout/stderr), then assert: 1. `goto` page → `#text` textContent equals `hello world` (use a fresh `DATA_FILE` env pointing at a temp file so the run is reproducible). 2. `page.on('console')` and `page.on('pageerror')` are collected for the whole run; **any `error`/`warning` or page error fails the run** (record it as evidence per VALIDATION §2). 3. Click `#text`, `page.keyboard.press('Control+A')`, type `hey you`, wait for the status pill to read `Saved` (≤2 s). 4. Assert `data/hello.json` (or the temp data file) on disk literally contains `hey you` — an artifact check independent of the UI. 5. `page.reload()` → `#text` reads `hey you`. 6. **Server restart proof:** close the server process, re-launch, `goto` again → still `hey you`. 7. New browser **context** (fresh profile, same server) → still `hey you` (proves cross-session, cross-profile persistence). 8. Keyboard-only path: from `about:blank`, `Tab` reaches `#text` and typing changes it. 9. Screenshots: `desktop-1440.png` (idle), `desktop-focus.png` (while editing), `mobile-390.png`, `desktop-reduced-motion.png` (with `reducedMotion: 'reduce'`); assert `document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= clientWidth` at both viewports. 10. Reduced-motion run: assert computed `animation-name` on a `.blob` is `none`. **Commands:** `node --test tests/` (unit+API) · `node /tmp/hello-e2e.mjs` (E2E) · `npm run check`. **Evidence to report** in the VALIDATION.md Completion Evidence block: each check PASS/FAIL with output, browser console output (must be empty), file contents of the data file, screenshot paths, and an explicit criterion-by-criterion acceptance table. --- ### 7. Documentation → outcome: a newcomer can run and test the app from the README alone **Files:** `README.md`, `docs/architecture.md` - `docs/architecture.md` (fill the template): module table (`main` → composition root, `server` → HTTP routing/API, `store` → the only filesystem owner, `public/*` → client), the dependency rule (`main → server → store`; `public/*` depends only on the HTTP contract; no back-edges, no cycles), the API contract table, and **two recorded compromises**: (a) explicit static asset map instead of a generic static handler — less code, no traversal risk, cost = one line per new asset; (b) last-write-wins single-user file store — trivially simple, cost = concurrent editors silently overwrite each other. - `README.md`: what it is, `npm start` (→ http://localhost:3000), `npm test`, `npm run check`, where data lives (`data/hello.json`, `DATA_FILE`/`PORT` overrides), and the limitation list (single user, no auth, one line). **Test:** every command in the README is copy-pasteable and actually works; `docs/architecture.md` matches the code as written. --- ## Acceptance criteria | # | Criterion | Evidence | |---|---|---| | A1 | `npm start` serves the app; `GET /` returns 200 HTML containing a `contenteditable` element | api test 1, manual curl, E2E step 1 | | A2 | A user can click the headline and edit it with the keyboard, seeing the change immediately | E2E steps 3 + 8, `desktop-focus.png` | | A3 | ≤1 s after the last keystroke the new text is on disk in the data file | E2E step 4 (`cat` the file) | | A4 | Text survives page reload, browser/server restart, and a fresh browser profile | E2E steps 5–7, api test 4 | | A5 | Visual spec items in step 5 all present (layered background + blobs + grain + vignette, gradient/glow `clamp()` type ≥ 12vw, status pill, visible focus ring, no horizontal scroll at 390 px) | 4 screenshots + human review | | A6 | Reduced-motion disables all animations | E2E step 10 | | A7 | Zero unexpected browser console/page errors during E2E | E2E step 2 log | | A8 | `node --test tests/` and `npm run check` pass | command output | | A9 | Stored content is rendered as text only (`textContent`); an edit containing `` is displayed literally, not executed | add an E2E step 11 typing that string and asserting it appears as literal text with no `dialog` event | ## Assumptions - **A1** "Persist across sessions" = server-side, shared by every browser/device and surviving server restarts (not per-browser `localStorage`). Rejected alternative: a static page with `localStorage` only — fewer moving parts, but invisible to automated verification and lost when the profile is cleared. If the requester actually wanted per-browser persistence with no backend, step 2/3 shrink to a single static file served by any static server; flag before building. - **A2** Node 26 (`node:http`, `node --test`) and the pre-installed Playwright 1.63 are the toolchain; nothing is installed. Python 3.14 exists but is unused. - **A3** Data file lives at `./data/hello.json` inside the repo (gitignored) for discoverability; overridable via `DATA_FILE`. - **A4** Single line of text, max 10 KB; Enter is suppressed. - **A5** Dark theme only; no i18n, no build step, no CI in scope. `init.txt` is left alone. ## Risks / open questions - **R1 Persistence semantics ambiguity** (A1 above) — cheapest thing to get wrong; the server-side choice is the safer superset but is more machinery than a pure client app. - **R2 "Visually stunning" is subjective.** Mitigated by the itemised visual spec in step 5 plus screenshots, but final judgement needs a human glance. Screenshot review is the weakest link in the evidence chain — disclose it rather than claim it as an objective pass. - **R3 Concurrency:** last-write-wins. Two open tabs silently overwrite each other. Accepted for a single-user demo; recorded in `docs/architecture.md`. - **R4 Playwright reachability:** importing from the mise global path is unusual; if it fails, E2E degrades to `curl` + file inspection + `playwright screenshot`, and DOM-level assertions (A2, A9) must be reported as *Not run* with the exact blocker, per VALIDATION "Blocked Validation". - **R5 No linter/formatter is configured in this repo** and none is added (no new dependencies). `node --check` is the only static gate; coding-standards' "standard formatter" requirement is unmet — surface this to the requester rather than silently adopting Prettier. - **R6 `contenteditable` quirks** (paste of rich text, IME composition, stray `
`). Mitigated by `plaintext-only` + `textContent` + suppressing Enter; IME composition is not exhaustively testable here — worth a manual check. - **R7 `-webkit-text-fill-color: transparent`** can hide the caret and is fragile in older engines; `caret-color` is set and a screenshot with focus proves caret visibility. ## Definition of done All steps 1–7 merged; `node --test tests/` green; `npm run check` green; Playwright E2E script passes with an empty console log; four screenshots reviewed; README + `docs/architecture.md` accurate; the Completion Evidence block from `docs/VALIDATION.md` produced, with anything not run explicitly disclosed. When finished, end your final message with a single JSON object that validates against this JSON Schema: ```json { "type": "object", "required": [ "summary" ], "properties": { "summary": { "type": "string", "description": "What was changed and why" } } } ```

# Architecture

Describe the modules of this system, their responsibilities and the allowed dependencies between them.
Record architectural compromises and their trade-offs here.
# Coding standards

- Keep functions small and single-purpose; name things for what they mean.
- No dead code, commented-out code or speculative abstractions.
- Every behaviour change has a test that exercises it.
- Errors are surfaced, never silently swallowed.
- Follow the language's standard formatter and linter.
# VALIDATION.md

Validation rules for coding agents. This file defines how an implemented change is proved correct and how validation failures are fed back into the coding loop.

> `AGENTS.md` defines **how agents engineer changes**.  
> `VALIDATION.md` defines **how agents prove those changes are correct**.

## Core Rule

**Implementation is not evidence. A change is complete only when the applicable validation demonstrates that the requested outcome was achieved without unacceptable regressions.**

Validation should be proportional to the change:
- Use the smallest useful checks while iterating.
- Expand validation as confidence grows.
- Run all applicable completion checks before declaring success.
- Not every validation category applies to every change.
- Higher-risk, broader or more user-visible changes require stronger evidence.

## Validation Feedback Loop

Use this loop for every non-trivial change:

```text
Define outcome
    ↓
Implement smallest change
    ↓
Run relevant validation
    ↓
Capture evidence
    ↓
Pass? ── yes ──→ Expand / final validation ──→ Complete
  │
  no
  ↓
Diagnose from failure evidence
    ↓
Feed precise failure back into coding
    ↓
Fix the cause
    ↓
Re-run the failed check
    └───────────────────────────────────────────↺
```

### 1. Define the expected outcome

Before validating, identify:
- The requested user-visible or system-visible outcome.
- The behaviour that must remain unchanged.
- Any explicit acceptance criteria.
- Relevant boundaries, failure cases and invariants.
- Which validation categories below are applicable.

Do not validate merely that code exists. Validate the behaviour the change was intended to produce.

### 2. Start with the narrowest useful check

During implementation:
- Run the smallest relevant test, command or observable check first.
- Prefer fast feedback over repeatedly running the entire suite.
- Where practical, create or update a test that expresses the changed behaviour.
- For bug fixes, reproduce the bug with a failing test or equivalent deterministic check before fixing it.
- Confirm new tests fail for the expected reason before relying on them as evidence.

### 3. Capture failure evidence

When validation fails, preserve the useful diagnostic information:
- Check or command that failed.
- Exit code or failure status.
- Relevant assertion, exception or compiler output.
- Browser console or page errors where applicable.
- Relevant logs or structured diagnostics.
- Expected behaviour versus observed behaviour.

Do not reduce a failure to "it didn't work" when more precise evidence is available.

### 4. Feed the failure back into the coding loop

Use validation output as the next coding input.

A useful failure report contains:

```text
Check:      [what was run]
Expected:   [what should have happened]
Observed:   [what actually happened]
Evidence:   [error/assertion/log/console output]
Cause:      [current diagnosis, if known]
Next step:  [smallest change likely to address the cause]
```

- Diagnose before editing.
- Fix the cause, not merely the symptom presented by the check.
- Keep the corrective change as small as possible.
- Do not introduce unrelated refactoring while fixing validation failures.
- If the failure exposes a wrong assumption, update the plan or acceptance criteria before continuing.

### 5. Re-run after every fix

After correcting a failure:
1. Re-run the failed check.
2. Run closely related checks that could have been affected.
3. Once local validation passes, expand to the broader applicable validation set.
4. Continue until all required checks pass or a genuine blocker is identified.

Never assume a fix worked because the code now looks plausible.

## Validation Categories

These categories form the validation toolbox. Select the ones applicable to the change and repository.

### 1. Build / Runtime

**Does the software actually compile, package, start and run?**

Validate as applicable:
- Compilation or build succeeds.
- Packaging succeeds.
- Application or service starts successfully.
- Changed commands or entry points execute.
- Migrations, generated artefacts or startup steps complete when relevant.
- Runtime does not immediately fail on the changed path.

Use the repository's existing build and run commands.

### 2. Observability

**Do runtime signals show the system behaving correctly and expose failures clearly?**

Inspect as applicable:
- Process output.
- Exceptions and stack traces.
- Structured logs.
- Browser console messages.
- API responses.
- Health or status endpoints.
- Background-task or integration diagnostics.

Treat unexpected errors as failures unless there is a specific, documented reason they are expected.

Observability is both a validation input and a design requirement: `AGENTS.md` requires code to expose enough useful state for validation to be possible.

### 3. Unit Tests

**Do individual functions, classes or modules exhibit the required behaviour in isolation?**

- Add or update meaningful coverage for changed behaviour.
- Test observable behaviour rather than implementation details.
- Include relevant happy paths, boundaries and failure paths.
- Keep tests deterministic where practical.
- Do not weaken, delete, skip or rewrite legitimate tests merely to make the implementation pass.
- During development, run the smallest relevant test set first.

### 4. Integration Tests

**Do connected components work correctly together?**

Validate interactions such as:
- Module-to-module contracts.
- Database access.
- File-system behaviour.
- Network or API boundaries.
- Queues, events or background workers.
- Framework integration.
- External-service adapters.

Prefer existing test fixtures, fakes, containers and repository conventions over inventing parallel infrastructure.

### 5. End-to-End Validation

**Does the complete user or system journey work through the real interface?**

For browser-based applications:
- Use Pi's built-in Playwright-compatible browser automation tools when available.
- Do not install Playwright, Chromium or other browser-testing packages solely for validation when the execution environment already provides browser automation.
- Exercise the changed behaviour through the user-facing interface.
- Capture browser console messages during validation.
- Treat unexpected browser console errors and unhandled page errors as failures.
- Do not ignore console errors without documenting a specific, justified exception.
- Do not add Playwright configuration, dependencies or committed test files unless the task explicitly requires them.
- If the repository already has a browser test suite, use its documented commands without changing dependencies unless a missing dependency is confirmed.

For non-browser systems, use the closest equivalent full journey through the public interface.

### 6. Linting

**Does the changed code conform to the project's static quality and style rules?**

Never:

- Ignore browser console or unhandled runtime errors without documenting why they are acceptable.
- Replace a meaningful assertion with a weaker one that no longer proves the behaviour.
- Mock away the behaviour that the validation is supposed to prove.
- Claim completion when required validation was not run.

- Continue only if the unrelated failure does not prevent meaningful validation of the requested change.

- State why it cannot run.
- Record any error or missing dependency.
- Do not install tools or change the environment until confirming the capability is not already available.
- Run the strongest remaining validation that is possible.
- Do not describe the task as fully validated.

Use a precise blocker rather than a vague caveat.

- [check]: PASS

Acceptance criteria
- [criterion]: PASS — [evidence]

Not run
- [check]: [reason, if applicable]

Blockers
- None
```

Only include checks that were actually run or explicitly assessed.

- No validation mechanism was weakened merely to obtain a pass.
- Any validation that could not be performed is clearly disclosed.
- There is no unresolved blocker being hidden behind a completion claim.

arguments.content:
# Architecture

Four server-side modules plus a browser client. The shape is deliberate: one composition
root, one HTTP layer, one (and only one) filesystem owner, and a client that knows nothing
about any of it except the HTTP contract.

## Modules

| Module | Responsibility | Public interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main.js` | Composition root. Reads `PORT` / `DATA_FILE`, builds the store, builds the server, listens, logs one startup line. No logic of its own. | executable (`npm start`) |
| `server.js` | HTTP routing and the JSON API: static assets, `GET/PUT /api/text`, status codes, error mapping, body-size limit. Never calls `listen()`. | `createServer(store) -> http.Server`, `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` |
| `store.js` | Persistence. The **only** module that touches the filesystem: read-or-default, atomic write (temp file + rename), default text. | `createFileStore(filePath) -> { read(), write(text) }`, `DEFAULT_TEXT` |
| `public/index.html`, `public/styles.css`, `public/app.js` | Client: renders the greeting in a `contenteditable`, debounces edits, saves over HTTP, reports save state. | the DOM it owns + the HTTP contract below |

## Dependency rule

```
main.js ──→ server.js ──→ (node:http, node:fs, node:path)
   │
   └──────→ store.js ←───┘   (server receives the store; main wires them together)

public/*  ──→ HTTP contract (GET/PUT /api/text) only
```

- `server.js` depends on the store's *contract* (`read`/`write`), never on `store.js` as a
  module — tests inject any object with those two methods.
- `store.js` depends on nothing in this codebase.
- `public/*` has no compile-time or runtime coupling to the server code: it only knows the
  two endpoints and the `{ "text": string }` shape.
- No back-edges, no cycles, no shared mutable globals. `main.js` is the only place the
  pieces are joined.

## HTTP contract

| Method | Path | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/` | `200` `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/styles.css` | `200` — `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/app.js` | `200` — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `200` `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → `200` `{"text":"<stored>"}` |
| any | other | `404` `{"error":"not found"}` |

Error semantics: unparseable JSON body or non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`;
body over `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` (10 000 bytes) → `413 {"error":"text too long"}`; a method other
than `GET`/`PUT` → `405` with an `Allow` header; an unexpected throw from the store →
`500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** a `console.error` carrying method, path and the error.

The on-disk format is the greeting as raw UTF-8 text in a single file (default
`data/hello.json`, overridable with `DATA_FILE`). The `.json` name is legacy naming only;
the content is intentionally plain text so that the file can be inspected with `cat`.

The XSS boundary is in the client: stored data is read and written through `textContent`
only, and the `contenteditable` element is `plaintext-only`. `innerHTML` is never used.

## Recorded compromises

**(a) Explicit static asset map instead of a generic static handler.**
`server.js` resolves `/`, `/styles.css` and `/app.js` from a literal table, reads each file
once at startup and serves the buffered bytes.
*Benefit:* roughly a dozen lines instead of a path-resolving handler, and zero path-traversal
surface — a request cannot escape the asset table no matter what it contains.
*Cost:* adding a static file means adding one deliberate line to `ASSETS` (and it is read at
startup, so a file added while the server runs needs a restart). Acceptable for three assets.

**(b) Last-write-wins single-user file store.**
`write()` overwrites the file unconditionally; there is no revision, ETag, lock or merge.
*Benefit:* the persistence layer is ~30 lines, has no state to get out of sync, and needs no
migration or schema.
*Cost:* two open tabs (or two people) editing at once silently overwrite each other — the
last save wins and the other edit is lost. Accepted for a single-user demo; the fix if it
ever matters is a revision field in the file plus a `409` on mismatch, which the current
store interface can absorb without touching `server.js`'s routing.

**Related invariants kept cheap on purpose:** the atomic write (temp file + `renameSync`)
exists so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated greeting; `read()` returns
`DEFAULT_TEXT` only for `ENOENT` and lets every other filesystem error propagate, so a real
IO problem is visible rather than silently reported as the default greeting.

**Not in scope:** authentication, sessions, multiple greetings, history/undo, a light theme,
user-selectable colours or fonts, i18n, a build step and CI.

# Architecture

Four server-side modules plus a browser client. The shape is deliberate: one composition
root, one HTTP layer, one (and only one) filesystem owner, and a client that knows nothing
about any of it except the HTTP contract.

## Modules

| Module | Responsibility | Public interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main.js` | Composition root. Reads `PORT` / `DATA_FILE`, builds the store, builds the server, listens, logs one startup line. No logic of its own. | executable (`npm start`) |
| `server.js` | HTTP routing and the JSON API: static assets, `GET/PUT /api/text`, status codes, error mapping, body-size limit. Never calls `listen()`. | `createServer(store) -> http.Server`, `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` |
| `store.js` | Persistence. The **only** module that touches the filesystem: read-or-default, atomic write (temp file + rename), default text. | `createFileStore(filePath) -> { read(), write(text) }`, `DEFAULT_TEXT` |
| `public/index.html`, `public/styles.css`, `public/app.js` | Client: renders the greeting in a `contenteditable`, debounces edits, saves over HTTP, reports save state. | the DOM it owns + the HTTP contract below |

## Dependency rule

```
main.js ──→ server.js ──→ (node:http, node:fs, node:path)
   │
   └──────→ store.js ←───┘   (server receives the store; main wires them together)

public/*  ──→ HTTP contract (GET/PUT /api/text) only
```

- `server.js` depends on the store's *contract* (`read`/`write`), never on `store.js` as a
  module — tests inject any object with those two methods.
- `store.js` depends on nothing in this codebase.
- `public/*` has no compile-time or runtime coupling to the server code: it only knows the
  two endpoints and the `{ "text": string }` shape.
- No back-edges, no cycles, no shared mutable globals. `main.js` is the only place the
  pieces are joined.

## HTTP contract

| Method | Path | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/` | `200` `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/styles.css` | `200` — `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/app.js` | `200` — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `200` `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → `200` `{"text":"<stored>"}` |
| any | other | `404` `{"error":"not found"}` |

Error semantics: unparseable JSON body or non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`;
body over `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` (10 000 bytes) → `413 {"error":"text too long"}`; a method other
than `GET`/`PUT` → `405` with an `Allow` header; an unexpected throw from the store →
`500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** a `console.error` carrying method, path and the error.

The on-disk format is the greeting as raw UTF-8 text in a single file (default
`data/hello.json`, overridable with `DATA_FILE`). The `.json` name is legacy naming only;
the content is intentionally plain text so that the file can be inspected with `cat`.

The XSS boundary is in the client: stored data is read and written through `textContent`
only, and the `contenteditable` element is `plaintext-only`. `innerHTML` is never used.

## Recorded compromises

**(a) Explicit static asset map instead of a generic static handler.**
`server.js` resolves `/`, `/styles.css` and `/app.js` from a literal table, reads each file
once at startup and serves the buffered bytes.
*Benefit:* roughly a dozen lines instead of a path-resolving handler, and zero path-traversal
surface — a request cannot escape the asset table no matter what it contains.
*Cost:* adding a static file means adding one deliberate line to `ASSETS` (and it is read at
startup, so a file added while the server runs needs a restart). Acceptable for three assets.

**(b) Last-write-wins single-user file store.**
`write()` overwrites the file unconditionally; there is no revision, ETag, lock or merge.
*Benefit:* the persistence layer is ~30 lines, has no state to get out of sync, and needs no
migration or schema.
*Cost:* two open tabs (or two people) editing at once silently overwrite each other — the
last save wins and the other edit is lost. Accepted for a single-user demo; the fix if it
ever matters is a revision field in the file plus a `409` on mismatch, which the current
store interface can absorb without touching `server.js`'s routing.

**Related invariants kept cheap on purpose:** the atomic write (temp file + `renameSync`)
exists so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated greeting; `read()` returns
`DEFAULT_TEXT` only for `ENOENT` and lets every other filesystem error propagate, so a real
IO problem is visible rather than silently reported as the default greeting.

**Not in scope:** authentication, sessions, multiple greetings, history/undo, a light theme,
user-selectable colours or fonts, i18n, a build step and CI.

   └──────→ store.js ←───┘   (server receives the store; main wires them together)

public/*  ──→ HTTP contract (GET/PUT /api/text) only
```

- `server.js` depends on the store's *contract* (`read`/`write`), never on `store.js` as a
  module — tests inject any object with those two methods.
- `store.js` depends on nothing in this codebase.
- `public/*` has no compile-time or runtime coupling to the server code: it only knows the
  two endpoints and the `{ "text": string }` shape.
- No back-edges, no cycles, no shared mutable globals. `main.js` is the only place the
  pieces are joined.

## HTTP contract

| Method | Path | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/` | `200` `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/styles.css` | `200` — `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/app.js` | `200` — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `200` `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → `200` `{"text":"<stored>"}` |
| any | other | `404` `{"error":"not found"}` |

Error semantics: unparseable JSON body or non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`;
body over `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` (10 000 bytes) → `413 {"error":"text too long"}`; a method other
than `GET`/`PUT` → `405` with an `Allow` header; an unexpected throw from the store →
`500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** a `console.error` carrying method, path and the error.

The on-disk format is the greeting as raw UTF-8 text in a single file (default
`data/hello.json`, overridable with `DATA_FILE`). The `.json` name is legacy naming only;
the content is intentionally plain text so that the file can be inspected with `cat`.

The XSS boundary is in the client: stored data is read and written through `textContent`
only, and the `contenteditable` element is `plaintext-only`. `innerHTML` is never used.

## Recorded compromises

**(a) Explicit static asset map instead of a generic static handler.**
`server.js` resolves `/`, `/styles.css` and `/app.js` from a literal table, reads each file
once at startup and serves the buffered bytes.
*Benefit:* roughly a dozen lines instead of a path-resolving handler, and zero path-traversal
surface — a request cannot escape the asset table no matter what it contains.
*Cost:* adding a static file means adding one deliberate line to `ASSETS` (and it is read at
startup, so a file added while the server runs needs a restart). Acceptable for three assets.

**(b) Last-write-wins single-user file store.**
`write()` overwrites the file unconditionally; there is no revision, ETag, lock or merge.
*Benefit:* the persistence layer is ~30 lines, has no state to get out of sync, and needs no
migration or schema.
*Cost:* two open tabs (or two people) editing at once silently overwrite each other — the
last save wins and the other edit is lost. Accepted for a single-user demo; the fix if it
ever matters is a revision field in the file plus a `409` on mismatch, which the current
store interface can absorb without touching `server.js`'s routing.

**Related invariants kept cheap on purpose:** the atomic write (temp file + `renameSync`)
exists so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated greeting; `read()` returns
`DEFAULT_TEXT` only for `ENOENT` and lets every other filesystem error propagate, so a real
IO problem is visible rather than silently reported as the default greeting.

**Not in scope:** authentication, sessions, multiple greetings, history/undo, a light theme,
user-selectable colours or fonts, i18n, a build step and CI.

# hello world

A single, large, animated **hello world** that you can click and edit. Whatever you type is
saved to the server, so it is still there after a reload, a browser restart, an incognito
window or a server restart.

No dependencies — Node's standard library on the server, plain ES modules in the browser.

## Run

```sh
npm start
```

Then open <http://localhost:3000>, click the headline and type. A small pill at the bottom
reports `Saving…` → `Saved HH:MM`. The greeting auto-saves about 400 ms after you stop
typing, and any unsaved keystrokes are flushed when the field loses focus or the tab closes.

Configuration (environment variables):

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `3000` | HTTP port |
| `DATA_FILE` | `./data/hello.json` | File holding the greeting |

## Test

```sh
npm test        # unit + HTTP API tests (node --test)
npm run check   # syntax check of every server file and the client script
```

## Where the data lives

`data/hello.json` (gitignored, created on first save). The file holds the greeting as plain
UTF-8 text, so it can be inspected directly:

```sh
cat data/hello.json
```

Delete the file (or the whole `data/` directory) to reset the greeting to `hello world`.

## HTTP API

| Method | Path | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"new text"}` → `{"text":"new text"}` |

```sh
curl -s localhost:3000/api/text
curl -s -X PUT -d '{"text":"bonjour"}' localhost:3000/api/text
```

## Limitations

- **Single user, last-write-wins.** Two open tabs edit the same string; the last save wins
  and the other edit is silently lost.
- **No authentication or authorisation.** Anyone who can reach the port can change the text.
- **One line of text, max 10 KB.** Enter is suppressed; a longer body is rejected with `413`.
- **Dark theme only**, no history/undo, no i18n, no build step.

See [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) for the module boundaries and the two
recorded compromises.

=== README ===
# hello world

A single, large, animated **hello world** that you can click and edit. Whatever you type is
saved to the server, so it is still there after a reload, a browser restart, an incognito
window or a server restart.

No dependencies — Node's standard library on the server, plain ES modules in the browser.

## Run

```sh
npm start
```

Then open <http://localhost:3000>, click the headline and type. A small pill at the bottom
reports `Saving…` → `Saved HH:MM`. The greeting auto-saves about 400 ms after you stop
typing, and any unsaved keystrokes are flushed when the field loses focus or the tab closes.

Configuration (environment variables):

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `3000` | HTTP port |
| `DATA_FILE` | `./data/hello.json` | File holding the greeting |

If something else already owns port 3000, pick another: `PORT=4173 npm start`.

## Test

```sh
npm test        # unit + HTTP API tests (node --test)
npm run check   # syntax check of every server file and the client script
```

## Where the data lives

`data/hello.json` (gitignored, created on first save). The file holds the greeting as plain
UTF-8 text, so it can be inspected directly:

```sh
cat data/hello.json
```

Delete the file (or the whole `data/` directory) to reset the greeting to `hello world`.

## HTTP API

| Method | Path | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"new text"}` → `{"text":"new text"}` |

```sh
curl -s localhost:3000/api/text
curl -s -X PUT -d '{"text":"bonjour"}' localhost:3000/api/text
```

## Limitations

- **Single user, last-write-wins.** Two open tabs edit the same string; the last save wins
  and the other edit is silently lost.
- **No authentication or authorisation.** Anyone who can reach the port can change the text.
- **One line of text, max ~10 KB.** Enter is suppressed; a request body over 10 000 bytes
  is rejected with `413`.
- **Dark theme only**, no history/undo, no i18n, no build step.

See [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) for the module boundaries and the two
recorded compromises.

Project-specific instructions and guidelines:

<project_instructions path="/home/ian/hello-world/AGENTS.md">
# AGENTS.md

Behavioural and engineering guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

**Trade-off:** These guidelines favour caution, clarity and verifiable progress over speed. Use judgement for trivial tasks.

> `AGENTS.md` defines **how agents engineer changes**.  
> `VALIDATION.md` defines **how agents prove those changes are correct**.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Do not assume. Do not hide confusion. Surface trade-offs.**

Before implementing:
- Inspect the relevant code, tests and repository conventions.
- Before installing any tool or dependency, check whether the required capability is already provided by the execution environment or the repository.
- State material assumptions explicitly.
- If multiple interpretations exist, identify them rather than choosing silently.
- Prefer the simplest interpretation consistent with the request.
- Record minor assumptions in `PLAN.md` when working autonomously.
- If a requirement is materially unclear or contradictory, stop and record the exact blocker rather than guessing.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so and push back when warranted.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Write the minimum code that solves the defined problem. Nothing speculative.**

- Do not add features beyond what was requested.
- Do not add speculative abstractions, extensibility, configuration or flexibility.
- Do not create interfaces, factories, wrappers or layers without a concrete need.
- Introduce an abstraction only when it removes meaningful duplication, isolates a volatile dependency, clarifies a responsibility or creates a necessary testing boundary.
- Do not add error handling for impossible scenarios.
- Prefer explicit control flow and simple data flow over hidden behaviour or excessive indirection.
- If a solution is substantially larger than necessary, simplify it.

Ask: "Would a senior engineer consider this overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what is required. Clean up only what your change makes obsolete.**

When editing existing code:
- Do not improve adjacent code, comments or formatting without need.
- Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Match the existing style and architecture unless the task explicitly changes them.
- Mention unrelated issues rather than fixing them.
- Keep architectural changes within the scope of the current plan step.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports, variables, functions and files made unused by your change.
- Do not remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

Every changed line should trace directly to the request or to work required to keep the change correct, coherent and maintainable.

## 4. Outcome-Driven Execution

**Understand the required outcome before deciding how to implement it.**

- Translate the request into a clear behavioural outcome.
- Identify constraints, invariants and affected public contracts.
- Distinguish the requested outcome from a suggested implementation approach.
- Prefer the smallest implementation that achieves the outcome.
- For multi-step work, create a brief `PLAN.md` and work one step at a time unless explicitly instructed otherwise.
- Keep each plan step independently understandable and small enough to reason about.
- Do not treat implementation activity as evidence of success; completion is governed by `VALIDATION.md`.

For multi-step work, a plan may use this shape:

```text
1. [Step] → outcome: [expected result]
2. [Step] → outcome: [expected result]
3. [Step] → outcome: [expected result]
```

## 5. Preserve Existing Behaviour

**Change the requested behaviour without accidentally changing unrelated behaviour.**

- Treat existing public behaviour as a constraint unless the task explicitly changes it.
- Preserve API contracts, data formats, configuration semantics and user-visible behaviour outside the requested scope.
- Avoid broad rewrites when a local change is sufficient.
- Consider downstream callers and consumers before changing shared code.
- Prefer backwards-compatible changes when compatibility is part of the existing contract.
- Do not silently change defaults, error semantics or side effects.
- If an intentional breaking change is required, make it explicit in the plan and implementation.

Ask: "What existing behaviour could this change accidentally disturb?"

## 6. Architecture and Design

**Prefer high cohesion, loose coupling and clear module boundaries.**

- Keep behaviour, data and tests that change for the same reason close together.
- Give each module a clear responsibility and a small, explicit public interface.
- Depend on contracts rather than implementation details where that improves replaceability or testability.
- Preserve encapsulation; internal changes should not force unrelated modules to change.
- Minimise knowledge between modules. A component should depend only on what it genuinely needs.
- Prefer composition over inheritance.
- Avoid circular dependencies.
- Avoid global mutable state and hidden dependencies.
- Use dependency injection or explicit parameters when they improve clarity and testability.
- Isolate external systems, network calls, databases, file systems, clocks and other non-deterministic dependencies behind clear boundaries.
- Keep business logic separate from frameworks, user interfaces, persistence and external services where practical.
- Extend an existing coherent abstraction rather than creating a parallel one.
- Remove duplication when it represents the same concept or rule; do not combine code that merely looks similar but changes for different reasons.
- Choose the simplest design that satisfies current requirements and remains straightforward to change.

Before implementing a change:
1. Identify the module that owns the behaviour.
2. Identify the public contract affected.
3. Identify external or non-deterministic dependencies that require isolation.
4. Identify where the change naturally belongs.
5. Prefer changing the owning module over spreading conditional logic across callers.

Document any necessary architectural compromise and its trade-off in `ARCHITECTURE.md`.

## 7. Context-Friendly Modularity

**Keep files focused. Split only at clear responsibility boundaries.**

- Keep each file focused on one clear purpose.
- Split large files when there is a natural responsibility boundary.
- Do not split code merely to reduce file length.
- Avoid tiny fragments that force readers or agents to chase context across many files.
- Prefer modules that are understandable in isolation.
- Keep related implementation, contracts and diagnostics easy to locate.
- Avoid structures that require loading large amounts of unrelated context to make a small change.

Ask: "Does this split reduce cognitive load, or merely move complexity around?" If it only moves complexity, keep it together.

## 8. Design for Observability

**Build systems so that their behaviour, failures and state can be inspected by both humans and coding agents.**

- Do not silently swallow errors or exceptions.
- Surface failures through an appropriate observable channel: process output, browser console, structured logging, files, API responses, test results or equivalent.
- Include enough diagnostic context to identify where and why a failure occurred.
- Prefer machine-readable diagnostic output where practical.
- Ensure important asynchronous, background and integration failures remain discoverable after they occur.
- Expose useful state or health information where behaviour cannot be inspected directly.
- Avoid requiring manual visual inspection as the only means of determining whether something worked.
- When adding a feature, consider how a coding agent will determine that it is working correctly and diagnose it when it is not.
- Make observable signals available to automated checks and CI/CD wherever practical.
- Do not add excessive logging or instrumentation without a concrete diagnostic or operational purpose.

Ask: "If this fails when no human is watching, can an agent determine what failed and why?"

## 9. Follow Existing Conventions

**Prefer the repository's established patterns over inventing new ones.**

- Reuse existing libraries, utilities, abstractions and project conventions where they are fit for purpose.
- Match existing naming, structure, formatting and error-handling patterns.
- Use the project's documented commands and workflows before introducing alternatives.
- Do not add a new dependency when the repository or execution environment already provides the capability.
- Do not introduce a second way of solving a problem unless there is a concrete reason.
- When conventions conflict with the requested change, make the conflict explicit rather than silently bypassing them.
- If a new pattern is genuinely required, keep it small, document why it exists and apply it consistently within the affected scope.

Ask: "Am I extending the system that is already here, or accidentally creating a parallel one?"

## 10. Validate Before Completion

**A change is not complete until the applicable validation defined in `VALIDATION.md` has passed.**

- Read and follow `VALIDATION.md` for the validation process, evidence requirements and feedback loop.
- Select validation checks according to the change, repository and risk; do not assume every check applies to every task.
- Do not declare success based on code inspection or plausibility alone.
- Do not weaken tests, suppress errors or bypass checks merely to make validation pass.
- When validation fails, use the failure evidence to diagnose and correct the implementation, then run the relevant checks again.
- If required validation cannot be run or cannot pass, record the precise blocker instead of claiming completion.

---

**These guidelines are working when:** diffs remain focused, designs stay simple, repository conventions are respected, systems are observable, architectural boundaries remain clear, unrelated behaviour is preserved, and completion claims are backed by the evidence required in `VALIDATION.md`.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

content.text:
Implement this plan in the repository. # Plan # Plan: Editable, persistent, visually striking Hello World web app ## Outcome A zero-dependency Node.js web app. Serving `GET /` shows a large, animated, full-viewport **hello world** that a visitor can click and edit in place. Every edit is saved to the server (debounced) into a JSON file on disk, so the text is still there after a page reload, a browser restart, an incognito window, or a server restart. ## Fixed design decisions (do not re-litigate during implementation) 1. **Server-side persistence to a file, not `localStorage`.** `localStorage` would satisfy 'persist across sessions' only per-browser and is invisible to automated verification. A file store gives an observable artifact (`data/hello.json`), survives server restarts and works across browsers/devices. See Risks R1 for the rejected alternative. 2. **Zero runtime and zero dev dependencies.** Node 26.8.1 is installed (mise) and provides `node:http`, `node:fs` and the built-in test runner `node --test`. Playwright 1.63.0 + Chromium 1228 are already installed globally (`~/.local/share/mise/installs/npm-playwright/1.63.0`, browsers in `~/.cache/ms-playwright`); `VALIDATION.md` explicitly forbids installing browser packages that already exist. Do not add React/Vite/Express/Tailwind/Prettier/ESLint. 3. **Editing via `contenteditable="plaintext-only"` on an `

`.** Read and write **only `textContent`**, never `innerHTML` — this is both the XSS boundary and what keeps stored data plain text. Browsers without `plaintext-only` fall back to `true`; since we always save/read `textContent`, pasted markup is flattened on save anyway. 4. **Single user, last-write-wins.** No auth, no sessions, no CRDT, no optimistic-concurrency ETags. Documented as an explicit assumption (R3). 5. **Default text is exactly `hello world`** (lowercase, one space). ## File layout to create ``` package.json # type=module, scripts: start | test | check ; no dependencies main.js # entry point: wires store + server, reads PORT/DATA_FILE env, listens store.js # file-backed text store: createFileStore(path) -> {read, write} server.js # createServer(store) -> http.Server ; routing + JSON API ; no listen() public/index.html # markup: h1#text contenteditable, status pill, layer elements public/app.js # load text, edit, debounced save, status indicator public/styles.css # the visual design (see Visual spec) tests/store.test.js # unit tests for the file store tests/api.test.js # HTTP integration tests via createServer + fetch on port 0 .gitignore # node_modules/, data/ README.md # how to run, how to test, data location, limitations docs/architecture.md # fill in the template: modules, contracts, dependency rule, compromise data/hello.json # runtime-created, gitignored ``` Do **not** touch `init.txt` (pre-existing, empty) or the other `docs/` files. --- ## Steps ### 1. Scaffold → outcome: `npm test` and `npm run check` run cleanly on an empty suite **Files:** `package.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.md` - `package.json`: `{ "name": "hello-world", "private": true, "type": "module", "scripts": { "start": "node main.js", "test": "node --test tests/", "check": "node --check store.js && node --check server.js && node --check main.js && node --check public/app.js" } }`. No `dependencies` / `devDependencies` keys at all. - `.gitignore`: `node_modules/` and `data/`. - `README.md`: title + placeholder Run/Test sections (completed in step 7). **Test:** `npm run check` exits 0 (may be a no-op until files exist — create them in later steps and re-run); `npm test` exits 0 with 0 tests. Commit scaffold. --- ### 2. Persistence layer → outcome: text round-trips to disk and survives re-instantiation **Files:** `store.js`, `tests/store.test.js` · **Write the tests first and watch them fail for the expected reason (missing module / missing export) before implementing.** Contract: ```js export const DEFAULT_TEXT = 'hello world' export function createFileStore(filePath) // -> { read(): string, write(text: string): void } ``` - `read()` — return the file contents as utf-8 string; if the file does not exist (`ENOENT`) return `DEFAULT_TEXT`. Any other `fs` error propagates (do **not** swallow it — AGENTS §8, coding-standards). - `write(text)` — `mkdirSync(dirname(filePath), { recursive: true })`, write to `filePath + '.tmp'`, then `renameSync` onto `filePath`. The temp+rename is deliberate: it prevents a truncated/corrupt `hello.json` if the process dies mid-write. Only a string is accepted; throw `TypeError` otherwise. - The store owns the path; nothing else in the codebase touches the filesystem. **Tests (`tests/store.test.js`, `node:test` + `node:assert`, each test uses `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(),'hello-'))` and cleans up):** 1. `read()` on a fresh empty dir returns `'hello world'`. 2. `write('bonjour')` then a **new** `createFileStore(samePath)` reads `'bonjour'` (proves on-disk persistence, not memory). 3. Unicode + newline round-trip: `'héllo 🌍\nline2'` survives write→read byte-for-byte. 4. `write()` creates missing parent directories (`data/nested/x.json`). 5. `read()` propagates a real IO error: point the store at a path whose parent is an existing *file*, assert `read()` throws (guards against silent error swallowing). 6. `write(42)` throws `TypeError`. **Test command:** `node --test tests/store.test.js` (all pass). --- ### 3. HTTP server + JSON API → outcome: `curl` can read and overwrite the greeting **Files:** `server.js`, `main.js`, `tests/api.test.js`, plus a one-line placeholder `public/index.html` (replaced in step 4) **Public contract (implement exactly):** | Method | Path | Response | |---|---|---| | GET | `/` | 200 `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/styles.css` | 200 — `text/css; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/app.js` | 200 — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` | | GET | `/api/text` | 200 `{"text":""}` | | PUT | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → 200 `{"text":""}` | | any | other | 404 `{"error":"not found"}` | Error semantics: PUT with unparseable JSON or a non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`. Body larger than `MAX_TEXT_BYTES = 10000` → `413 {"error":"text too long"}` (stop accumulating and consume the rest). Method other than GET/PUT on any path → `405` with an `Allow` header. An unexpected throw from the store → `500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** `console.error` including method, path and the error (never silent). Structure: `server.js` exports `createServer(store)` returning an `http.Server` and never calls `listen` (keeps it testable). # Architecture

Describe the modules of this system, their responsibilities and the allowed dependencies between them.
Record architectural compromises and their trade-offs here.
# Coding standards

- Keep functions small and single-purpose; name things for what they mean.
- No dead code, commented-out code or speculative abstractions.
- Every behaviour change has a test that exercises it.
- Errors are surfaced, never silently swallowed.
- Follow the language's standard formatter and linter.
# VALIDATION.md

Validation rules for coding agents. This file defines how an implemented change is proved correct and how validation failures are fed back into the coding loop.

> `AGENTS.md` defines **how agents engineer changes**.  
> `VALIDATION.md` defines **how agents prove those changes are correct**.

## Core Rule

**Implementation is not evidence. A change is complete only when the applicable validation demonstrates that the requested outcome was achieved without unacceptable regressions.**

Validation should be proportional to the change:
- Use the smallest useful checks while iterating.
- Expand validation as confidence grows.
- Run all applicable completion checks before declaring success.
- Not every validation category applies to every change.
- Higher-risk, broader or more user-visible changes require stronger evidence.

## Validation Feedback Loop

Use this loop for every non-trivial change:

```text
Define outcome
    ↓
Implement smallest change
    ↓
Run relevant validation
    ↓
Capture evidence
    ↓
Pass? ── yes ──→ Expand / final validation ──→ Complete
  │
  no
  ↓
Diagnose from failure evidence
    ↓
Feed precise failure back into coding
    ↓
Fix the cause
    ↓
Re-run the failed check
    └───────────────────────────────────────────↺
```

### 1. Define the expected outcome

Before validating, identify:
- The requested user-visible or system-visible outcome.
- The behaviour that must remain unchanged.
- Any explicit acceptance criteria.
- Relevant boundaries, failure cases and invariants.
- Which validation categories below are applicable.

Do not validate merely that code exists. Validate the behaviour the change was intended to produce.

### 2. Start with the narrowest useful check

During implementation:
- Run the smallest relevant test, command or observable check first.
- Prefer fast feedback over repeatedly running the entire suite.
- Where practical, create or update a test that expresses the changed behaviour.
- For bug fixes, reproduce the bug with a failing test or equivalent deterministic check before fixing it.
- Confirm new tests fail for the expected reason before relying on them as evidence.

### 3. Capture failure evidence

When validation fails, preserve the useful diagnostic information:
- Check or command that failed.
- Exit code or failure status.
- Relevant assertion, exception or compiler output.
- Browser console or page errors where applicable.
- Relevant logs or structured diagnostics.
- Expected behaviour versus observed behaviour.

Do not reduce a failure to "it didn't work" when more precise evidence is available.

### 4. Feed the failure back into the coding loop

Use validation output as the next coding input.

A useful failure report contains:

```text
Check:      [what was run]
Expected:   [what should have happened]
Observed:   [what actually happened]
Evidence:   [error/assertion/log/console output]
Cause:      [current diagnosis, if known]
Next step:  [smallest change likely to address the cause]
```

- Diagnose before editing.
- Fix the cause, not merely the symptom presented by the check.
- Keep the corrective change as small as possible.
- Do not introduce unrelated refactoring while fixing validation failures.
- If the failure exposes a wrong assumption, update the plan or acceptance criteria before continuing.

### 5. Re-run after every fix

After correcting a failure:
1. Re-run the failed check.
2. Run closely related checks that could have been affected.
3. Once local validation passes, expand to the broader applicable validation set.
4. Continue until all required checks pass or a genuine blocker is identified.

Never assume a fix worked because the code now looks plausible.

## Validation Categories

These categories form the validation toolbox. Select the ones applicable to the change and repository.

### 1. Build / Runtime

**Does the software actually compile, package, start and run?**

Validate as applicable:
- Compilation or build succeeds.
- Packaging succeeds.
- Application or service starts successfully.
- Changed commands or entry points execute.
- Migrations, generated artefacts or startup steps complete when relevant.
- Runtime does not immediately fail on the changed path.

Use the repository's existing build and run commands.

### 2. Observability

**Do runtime signals show the system behaving correctly and expose failures clearly?**

Inspect as applicable:
- Process output.
- Exceptions and stack traces.
- Structured logs.
- Browser console messages.
- API responses.
- Health or status endpoints.
- Background-task or integration diagnostics.

Treat unexpected errors as failures unless there is a specific, documented reason they are expected.

Observability is both a validation input and a design requirement: `AGENTS.md` requires code to expose enough useful state for validation to be possible.

### 3. Unit Tests

**Do individual functions, classes or modules exhibit the required behaviour in isolation?**

- Add or update meaningful coverage for changed behaviour.
- Test observable behaviour rather than implementation details.
- Include relevant happy paths, boundaries and failure paths.
- Keep tests deterministic where practical.
- Do not weaken, delete, skip or rewrite legitimate tests merely to make the implementation pass.
- During development, run the smallest relevant test set first.

### 4. Integration Tests

**Do connected components work correctly together?**

Validate interactions such as:
- Module-to-module contracts.
- Database access.
- File-system behaviour.
- Network or API boundaries.
- Queues, events or background workers.
- Framework integration.
- External-service adapters.

Prefer existing test fixtures, fakes, containers and repository conventions over inventing parallel infrastructure.

### 5. End-to-End Validation

**Does the complete user or system journey work through the real interface?**

For browser-based applications:
- Use Pi's built-in Playwright-compatible browser automation tools when available.
- Do not install Playwright, Chromium or other browser-testing packages solely for validation when the execution environment already provides browser automation.
- Exercise the changed behaviour through the user-facing interface.
- Capture browser console messages during validation.
- Treat unexpected browser console errors and unhandled page errors as failures.
- Do not ignore console errors without documenting a specific, justified exception.
- Do not add Playwright configuration, dependencies or committed test files unless the task explicitly requires them.
- If the repository already has a browser test suite, use its documented commands without changing dependencies unless a missing dependency is confirmed.

For non-browser systems, use the closest equivalent full journey through the public interface.

### 6. Linting

**Does the changed code conform to the project's static quality and style rules?**

Treat security validation proportionally to risk. Do not claim a security property that has not actually been checked.

### 11. Architectural Conformance

**Does the change preserve the intended module boundaries, dependency rules and design constraints?**

Check as applicable:
- No forbidden dependency directions.
- No new circular dependencies.
- Public contracts remain coherent.
- Business logic remains in the intended layer.
- External systems remain behind defined boundaries.
- New code extends existing abstractions rather than creating accidental parallel architectures.
- Repository-specific architectural fitness rules still pass.

Automate these checks where the repository provides tooling; otherwise inspect the affected dependency and module boundaries explicitly.

### 12. Acceptance Criteria

**Does the final behaviour explicitly satisfy what was requested?**

This is the final outcome check.

For each acceptance criterion:
- State the criterion.
- Identify the evidence that demonstrates it.
- Confirm whether it passed.
- Do not substitute passing technical checks for the requested user outcome.

A build can pass while the feature is still wrong. Acceptance validation closes that gap.

## Validation Order

Use a fast-to-broad sequence where practical:

```text
Focused check
→ Unit
→ Static checks
→ Integration
→ Build / runtime
→ E2E
→ Architecture / security / quality gates
→ Acceptance criteria
```

The exact order depends on the repository and change. Fail fast with cheap checks before running expensive ones.

## Do Not Game Validation

Never:
- Delete or weaken a legitimate test because the implementation fails it.
- Mark a test skipped solely to obtain a green result.
- Suppress compiler, type, lint, security or runtime errors without a justified reason.
- Change thresholds merely because the new code exceeds them.
- Ignore browser console or unhandled runtime errors without documenting why they are acceptable.
- Replace a meaningful assertion with a weaker one that no longer proves the behaviour.
- Mock away the behaviour that the validation is supposed to prove.
- Claim completion when required validation was not run.

If a validation rule itself is wrong, treat changing that rule as a separate, explicit engineering decision.

## Existing Failures

If validation reveals a failure that predates the current change:
- Confirm that it is genuinely pre-existing where possible.
- Do not silently fix unrelated failures.
- Record the failure and the evidence that it is unrelated.
- Ensure the current change has not made it worse.
- Continue only if the unrelated failure does not prevent meaningful validation of the requested change.

## Blocked Validation

If a required check cannot be run:
- State exactly which check is blocked.
- State why it cannot run.
- Record any error or missing dependency.
- Do not install tools or change the environment until confirming the capability is not already available.
- Run the strongest remaining validation that is possible.
- Do not describe the task as fully validated.

Use a precise blocker rather than a vague caveat.

## Completion Evidence

Before declaring work complete, summarise the evidence concisely:

```text
Validation
- [check]: PASS
- [check]: PASS
- [check]: PASS

Acceptance criteria
- [criterion]: PASS — [evidence]

Not run
- [check]: [reason, if applicable]

Blockers
- None
```

Only include checks that were actually run or explicitly assessed.

## Definition of Done

A coding change is complete when:
- The requested outcome is implemented.
- Applicable validation checks pass.
- Relevant regressions have been checked.
- Acceptance criteria are explicitly demonstrated.
- Unexpected runtime, browser or diagnostic errors have been resolved or justified.
- No validation mechanism was weakened merely to obtain a pass.
- Any validation that could not be performed is clearly disclosed.
- There is no unresolved blocker being hidden behind a completion claim.

---

**This validation process is working when:** failures generate actionable evidence, that evidence drives the next coding step, fixes are re-tested rather than assumed, validation expands with confidence, and agents only declare success when the requested outcome is supported by passing evidence.

# Architecture

Four server-side modules plus a browser client. The shape is deliberate: one composition
root, one HTTP layer, one (and only one) filesystem owner, and a client that knows nothing
about any of it except the HTTP contract.

## Modules

| Module | Responsibility | Public interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main.js` | Composition root. Reads `PORT` / `DATA_FILE`, builds the store, builds the server, listens, logs one startup line. No logic of its own. | executable (`npm start`) |
| `server.js` | HTTP routing and the JSON API: static assets, `GET/PUT /api/text`, status codes, error mapping, body-size limit. Never calls `listen()`. | `createServer(store) -> http.Server`, `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` |
| `store.js` | Persistence. The **only** module that touches the filesystem: read-or-default, atomic write (temp file + rename), default text. | `createFileStore(filePath) -> { read(), write(text) }`, `DEFAULT_TEXT` |
| `public/index.html`, `public/styles.css`, `public/app.js` | Client: renders the greeting in a `contenteditable`, debounces edits, saves over HTTP, reports save state. | the DOM it owns + the HTTP contract below |

## Dependency rule

```
main.js ──→ server.js ──→ (node:http, node:fs, node:path)
   │
   └──────→ store.js ←───┘   (server receives the store; main wires them together)

public/*  ──→ HTTP contract (GET/PUT /api/text) only
```

- `server.js` depends on the store's *contract* (`read`/`write`), never on `store.js` as a
  module — tests inject any object with those two methods.
- `store.js` depends on nothing in this codebase.
- `public/*` has no compile-time or runtime coupling to the server code: it only knows the
  two endpoints and the `{ "text": string }` shape.
- No back-edges, no cycles, no shared mutable globals. `main.js` is the only place the
  pieces are joined.

## HTTP contract

| Method | Path | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/` | `200` `public/index.html` — `text/html; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/styles.css` | `200` — `text/css; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/app.js` | `200` — `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` |
| `GET` | `/api/text` | `200` `{"text":"<current>"}` |
| `PUT` | `/api/text` | body `{"text":"..."}` → `200` `{"text":"<stored>"}` |
| any | other | `404` `{"error":"not found"}` |

Error semantics: unparseable JSON body or non-string `text` → `400 {"error":"text must be a string"}`;
body over `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` (10 000 bytes) → `413 {"error":"text too long"}`; a method other
than `GET`/`PUT` → `405` with an `Allow` header; an unexpected throw from the store →
`500 {"error":"internal"}` **and** a `console.error` carrying method, path and the error.

The on-disk format is the greeting as raw UTF-8 text in a single file (default
`data/hello.json`, overridable with `DATA_FILE`). The `.json` name is legacy naming only;
the content is intentionally plain text so that the file can be inspected with `cat`.

The XSS boundary is in the client: stored data is read and written through `textContent`
only, and the `contenteditable` element is `plaintext-only`. `innerHTML` is never used.

## Recorded compromises

**(a) Explicit static asset map instead of a generic static handler.**
`server.js` resolves `/`, `/styles.css` and `/app.js` from a literal table, reads each file
once at startup and serves the buffered bytes.
*Benefit:* roughly a dozen lines instead of a path-resolving handler, and zero path-traversal
surface — a request cannot escape the asset table no matter what it contains.
*Cost:* adding a static file means adding one deliberate line to `ASSETS` (and it is read at
startup, so a file added while the server runs needs a restart). Acceptable for three assets.

**(b) Last-write-wins single-user file store.**
`write()` overwrites the file unconditionally; there is no revision, ETag, lock or merge.
*Benefit:* the persistence layer is ~30 lines, has no state to get out of sync, and needs no
migration or schema.
*Cost:* two open tabs (or two people) editing at once silently overwrite each other — the
last save wins and the other edit is lost. Accepted for a single-user demo; the fix if it
ever matters is a revision field in the file plus a `409` on mismatch, which the current
store interface can absorb without touching `server.js`'s routing.

**Related invariants kept cheap on purpose:** the atomic write (temp file + `renameSync`)
exists so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated greeting; `read()` returns
`DEFAULT_TEXT` only for `ENOENT` and lets every other filesystem error propagate, so a real
IO problem is visible rather than silently reported as the default greeting.

**Not in scope:** authentication, sessions, multiple greetings, history/undo, a light theme,
user-selectable colours or fonts, i18n, a build step and CI.
